outputs.L2:
It may seem strange, but in 1985, as I readied Dan White’s body for burial, his fragile hands rested in mine. By that time, the years following Harvey Milk’s assassination had transformed Milk into a monument—more than that, into a myth.

I was twenty when Harvey was killed, and I already knew I was queer. Back then, men in Levi’s and leather jackets walked hand in hand along Castro Street, rallying behind Milk, who won election on the very same day as White.

My thoughts often return to Supervisor White, the man who murdered Mayor Moscone and Supervisor Milk—Milk, a Castro queer, one of our own. On May 21, 1979, a jury sentenced White, a former police officer and firefighter, to seven years, though he actually served five, despite the blood on his hands. When he admitted to shooting both the mayor and the queer supervisor, some men in blue applauded.

And what of Harvey Milk? For years, some people suggested, not quite openly, that there was no reason to mourn “spilled milk.” What they meant was simple: there was now “one less queer.”

The jurors placed their attention on White. Had he killed only the mayor, he might have faced serious consequences. But perhaps the twelve people holding his fate in their hands were untroubled by Milk’s death; perhaps that second killing even helped White escape with only a few years in prison.

Dan White ultimately died by suicide. And in the end, it was a queer who prepared his body for viewing.
outputs.L3:
In 1985, a queer narrator was assigned the task of preparing Dan White’s body for burial. Years earlier, White had assassinated San Francisco Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk, one of the nation’s first openly gay elected officials. The narrator recalls having embraced a queer identity at the age of twenty and celebrating Milk’s election with San Francisco’s Castro community, where his victory represented hope, visibility, and political progress.

That hope was shattered by the murders and their aftermath. Although White confessed to killing both Moscone and Milk, he received a notably lenient sentence. Reports that some police officers cheered his actions further reflected the hostility surrounding Milk and the broader queer community. The text suggests that pervasive homophobia diminished the perceived value of Milk’s life and may have helped create the conditions in which White was punished less severely than many believed justice required.

After White later died by suicide, the narrator confronted a grim irony: the man responsible for killing an important queer leader was ultimately made presentable for burial by a queer person. This final encounter transforms the preparation of White’s body into a powerful reflection on violence, prejudice, justice, and the unexpected intimacy of death.
outputs.L4:
I remember Dan White first as a body.

By the time he arrived at the funeral home, the shouting that had surrounded his name for years had gone quiet. There were no television cameras in the preparation room, no police officers guarding the doors, no crowds chanting in the streets. There was only the ordinary machinery of death: stainless steel, white towels, bottles arranged in rows, the low hum of ventilation. And there was me, a queer mortician, entrusted with the care of the man who had killed Harvey Milk.

Death had made White defenseless, but it had not made him innocent. As I prepared him for burial, I could not separate the body before me from the history attached to it. My hands followed the practiced rituals of the profession—washing, shaving, dressing, restoring—but my thoughts returned to San Francisco in 1977, when both White and Milk were elected to the Board of Supervisors.

Their victories represented very different visions of the city. Milk’s election was historic. He did not conceal his sexuality or ask gay people to make themselves less visible in exchange for tolerance. He insisted that visibility was political power. He urged queer people to come out because secrecy allowed others to pretend we did not exist. His campaigns drew energy from shopkeepers, laborers, young activists, lesbians, gay men, and people who had been told that public life did not belong to them. When he took office, he carried their hopes with him.

White came from another San Francisco. A former police officer and firefighter, he presented himself as a guardian of traditional neighborhoods and conventional values. He spoke for constituents who believed their city was changing too quickly and who feared the political strength of communities that had long been excluded. White and Milk could sometimes work together, but they also stood on opposite sides of the city’s cultural transformation.

In November 1978, overwhelmed by financial pressures and political frustration, White resigned from the board. Soon afterward, he changed his mind and asked Mayor George Moscone to reappoint him. Moscone initially considered doing so, then decided against it. On November 27, White entered City Hall through a basement window, avoiding the metal detectors. He carried a loaded revolver and extra ammunition.

He went first to Moscone’s office. After a brief conversation, White shot the mayor. He then reloaded, walked to Milk’s office, and shot him too.

The killings were not random explosions of rage. White had armed himself, bypassed security, confronted both men, and fired multiple times. Yet the legal system would later describe his responsibility in diminished terms. His attorneys argued that severe depression had impaired his judgment. References to his changed eating habits—including his consumption of junk food—helped produce the popular phrase “Twinkie defense,” though sugar itself was never formally offered as the cause of the murders. The larger argument was that White lacked the capacity for premeditation required for a murder conviction.

The jury convicted him of voluntary manslaughter rather than murder. He received a sentence of seven years and eight months and served about five years.

For many queer people, the verdict felt like a declaration that Milk’s life—and Moscone’s—had been assigned a lower value. The anger that erupted outside City Hall during the White Night riots was not simply grief over one trial. It came from accumulated knowledge: queer people could be beaten, discarded, or killed, while institutions searched for reasons to understand their attackers. The law could find endless complexity in the mind of the killer and very little humanity in the person killed.

Police responded to the protests with violence, striking demonstrators and later raiding a gay bar in the Castro. Once again, the state’s sympathy seemed to flow in one direction. White’s despair was treated as mitigating. Queer rage was treated as a threat.

Years later, after his release from prison, White returned to San Francisco. In 1985, he died by suicide from carbon monoxide poisoning. That was how he came to the funeral home and, eventually, to my table.

I had learned not to confuse care with forgiveness. A mortician’s work is intimate, but it is not absolution. We serve the dead partly for the sake of the living. We close mouths, smooth collars, and soften the visible evidence of death so that families can recognize the person they loved. The dead cannot thank us, and they cannot refuse us. In that room, power takes a strange form. The body is helpless; the mortician bears responsibility.

Still, the irony was impossible to ignore. A queer person was giving tenderness and dignity to the remains of the man who had taken Harvey Milk from us. White had helped create a world in which queer bodies were treated as expendable, yet his own body was being handled with patience by someone whose life belonged to the community Milk had represented.

I wondered what White would have thought if he had known who was preparing him. Perhaps it would have disturbed him. Perhaps, by the end of his life, it would not have mattered. There was no answer available in his face. Death had erased argument but not consequence.

So I continued my work.

I did not do it because I believed he deserved more mercy than Milk had received. I did it because my humanity was not his to determine. The care I gave him did not revise the verdict, excuse the killings, or heal the wounds left by that November morning. It testified instead to something White’s violence had failed to destroy: queer people were still here, still working, still remembering, still capable of choosing what kind of people we would be.

When I finished, Dan White looked peaceful. That peace was an illusion created by professional hands. History remained unsettled. Harvey Milk was still dead. George Moscone was still dead. A lenient sentence still stood as evidence of whose pain the system had been prepared to understand.

I covered White’s body and turned off the light. I had made him presentable for burial, but I had not buried what he had done.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person creative nonfiction monologue from the perspective of a queer mortician who prepared Dan White’s body for burial in 1985 and reflects on Harvey Milk’s assassination, the lenient verdict, and the homophobia surrounding the case.
counterfactuals.output:
*The following is a fictionalized monologue grounded in historical events.*

---

They brought Dan White to me in October of 1985.

There are names that enter a mortuary before the body does. His had been in the room for years.

White. Former policeman. Former fireman. Former supervisor. The man who climbed through a basement window at City Hall with a revolver and extra ammunition. The man who shot Mayor George Moscone, reloaded, then crossed the building and shot Harvey Milk.

Five bullets for Harvey. Two in the head.

I knew all of that before I unzipped the bag.

A mortician is supposed to receive the dead without judgment. We wash them. We close their eyes and mouths. We return shape to whatever death has disordered. Grief pays us to create one final, bearable fiction: that the person is only sleeping and might wake if called by the right voice.

The dead do not arrive innocent. But they do arrive helpless.

So I worked.

White had killed himself in his garage with carbon monoxide, less than two years after leaving prison. People were already calling his death tragic. They always find that word quickly for certain men.

I remember looking at his hands. That is what stays with me. Not the face. Hands are intimate in a way faces are not. Faces rehearse. Hands confess. I thought: These are the hands that carried the gun. These fingers pulled the trigger, and pulled it again, and again.

Then I cleaned beneath the nails.

That was my profession. That was my promise.

But beneath the white coat, beneath the practiced calm, I was one of the people Harvey had taught to step into the light.

I did not know Harvey Milk personally. That matters to say. Death has a way of manufacturing intimacies. People begin speaking of public figures as though they shared breakfast. I never sat across from Harvey. I never heard him argue over coffee or watched him lose patience in a grocery line.

But I knew what his existence had done.

He spoke as if we were not an embarrassment to be managed. He told us to come out because silence was the closet’s lock. He made queerness sound not merely survivable but civic—a thing that belonged in chambers, on ballots, before microphones. He said hope had to be given, and for a while it seemed he had found a way to hand it out like bread.

Then Dan White entered City Hall.

At the trial, the defense argued diminished capacity. Depression. Pressure. A life coming apart. The newspapers seized on the junk food—the famous “Twinkie defense”—though the sweets were presented as evidence of his decline, not the cause of the killings. The phrase made the whole thing sound absurd, almost comic.

Nothing about the verdict felt comic.

Not guilty of murder. Guilty of voluntary manslaughter.

Seven years and eight months for killing two men. He served about five.

Five years.

There are embalming chemicals that take longer to leave the soil.

When the verdict came down, San Francisco erupted. The White Night riots, they called them. Police cars burned. City Hall’s windows broke. Later, officers stormed the Castro, swinging clubs in a neighborhood already raw with grief.

People asked why everyone was so angry.

That question was its own cruelty.

We were angry because we had watched the world assign different weights to different lives. Because Harvey was not only dead; he was being made killable after the fact. Because every mention of his sexuality carried an insinuation, as though being openly gay were itself a provocation. Because White’s disappointment, his wounded pride, his depression, were granted narrative depth, while our fear was treated as hysteria.

The jury saw a troubled man.

We saw the old permission.

You may hate them. You may strike them. You may kill them. And afterward the world will search your childhood, your diet, your marriage, your mood—anything that might make your hand seem less connected to the weapon.

As I prepared White, I wondered what mercy meant.

Was it mercy to make him presentable for his family? Yes. I believe it was.

Was it forgiveness? No.

The two are not the same, though people often confuse them when they want the injured to become quiet.

I set his features. I dressed him. I arranged him in the casket so those who loved him could recognize the man they remembered instead of the man the garage had returned. Somewhere, perhaps, his family carried a version of him untouched by City Hall. The dead are rarely only one thing to those who mourn them.

Neither are their victims.

Harvey was not a saint made of campaign posters. He was ambitious, theatrical, stubborn. He could be difficult. I am grateful for that. Saints are easy to admire and impossible to resemble. Harvey was a man, and that was the point. An ordinary, complicated queer man had the right to stand in public and wield power. He had the right to be imperfect and remain alive.

I sometimes imagined Harvey on my table instead.

Another mortuary prepared him after the autopsy. Someone else washed the blood from his hair. Someone else confronted the damage bullets do when fired at close range. Someone else tried to make violence look like sleep.

That is the obscenity hidden inside my trade: murder creates work for careful hands.

I gave Dan White the dignity I would want given to any dead person, including Harvey, including myself. I did it not because White had earned more compassion than his victims, but because my ethics could not depend on his.

Yet I will not pretend my hands were serene.

As I fastened his collar, I thought of the men who had called me names in school. The landlord who once asked whether my “friend” would be staying often. The patients whose families lowered their voices when they described an unmarried brother. I thought of every queer funeral where grief had to disguise itself—lovers introduced as roommates, partners seated behind blood relatives, whole lives edited at the casket.

Homophobia does not always arrive shouting. Sometimes it speaks in courtroom language. Sometimes it wears a badge. Sometimes it sits on a jury and calls hatred something softer. Sometimes it appears in an obituary by omitting the name of the person who shared the bed.

And sometimes it is simply the confidence that our deaths will require less explanation than our lives.

When I finished, Dan White looked peaceful.

That word again: a mortuary word, a lie we tell tenderly.

I stood beside the casket and allowed myself one private sentence.

*Harvey should have grown old.*

Then I turned off the light.

The dead man kept his silence. The city did not.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical historical essay about the irony of a gay funeral worker holding Dan White’s hands after his suicide, years after White murdered Harvey Milk and George Moscone. Use repetition and wordplay involving “hands,” “shot,” and “spilled milk.”
counterfactuals.output:
The dead man’s hands were quiet at last.

They were the hands of Dan White: former police officer, former firefighter, former San Francisco supervisor; the hands that had carried a revolver through a basement window of City Hall on November 27, 1978; the hands that had loaded, aimed, fired, reloaded. White shot Mayor George Moscone. Then he crossed the building and shot Supervisor Harvey Milk, one of the first openly gay elected officials in the United States.

Seven years later, after White died by suicide, a gay funeral worker held those hands.

History sometimes compresses itself into a gesture. A city’s grief, a community’s rage, a courtroom’s failure—all of it can seem to gather in the space between one living palm and one dead one. The funeral worker’s hands performed the final office that White’s had denied to others: they tended rather than destroyed, arranged rather than shattered. They held without taking hold.

Hand over hand, history passes down its injuries.

White’s shots did not stop at two bodies. They passed through San Francisco’s civic faith. They struck the gay community’s fragile hope that public visibility might bring public safety. They echoed through the trial, where White was convicted not of murder but of voluntary manslaughter, a verdict so widely viewed as lenient that the city erupted in the White Night riots. Police cars burned near City Hall. Police retaliated in the Castro. Windows broke. Blood spilled. The city took another shot at justice and missed.

Harvey Milk had understood the danger of public life, especially gay public life. He had recorded a message to be played if he were assassinated. “If a bullet should enter my brain,” he said, “let that bullet destroy every closet door.” The line turns the assassin’s shot against itself: one shot, then an opening; one death, then thousands of lives refusing concealment. Milk knew that a body could be stopped while a voice kept moving.

And so “spilled milk” becomes an unbearable phrase. The old proverb commands resignation: there is no use crying over spilled milk. But this was Milk, capitalized by history, and crying was useful. Crying was testimony. Crying filled the streets with candlelight. Crying named what had been lost and what must not be surrendered. Milk was spilled on the floor of City Hall, but his hope could not be wiped away. The city cried over Milk because not to cry would have been another kind of forgetting.

Moscone, too, must not disappear behind the brighter afterlife of Milk’s name. He was a mayor of coalitions, a man whose politics helped make room for people long kept outside the civic frame. White shot Moscone first. The sequence matters because both men belonged to the same contested future: a city becoming more various, more visible, less obedient to older hierarchies. The shots were personal acts with public consequences.

Then came White’s own death in 1985, not by a gunshot but by carbon monoxide in a closed garage. No courtroom waited this time. No jury would weigh motive against damage. His body passed instead into the hands of funeral workers—the anonymous custodians who meet emperors and outcasts, victims and killers at the same final level.

Among those hands were the hands of a gay man.

What did it mean for him to hold White’s hands? Not forgiveness, necessarily. Not absolution. The work of the dead does not demand that the living forget. A funeral worker may close a mouth without silencing history, smooth a sleeve without smoothing over guilt. Professional care is not pardon. Mercy is not amnesia.

Yet there is a fierce irony in the touch. White had helped make gay San Franciscans feel hunted; now a gay man handled him gently. White’s hands had delivered death; the worker’s hands prepared the dead. One pair had been armed by grievance. The other was armed only with duty.

Hands can fire a shot. Hands can light candles after the shot. Hands can smash windows, swing batons, write verdicts, carry coffins, cast ballots. Hands can clasp in mourning or rise in protest. They can spill blood. They can clean what has been spilled.

And sometimes they can hold the hands that caused the spilling.

That final contact does not redeem Dan White. It reveals something about the community he wounded. The gay funeral worker’s care was not surrender but proof of a moral world larger than White’s violence. It was a small, private mastery over hatred: the dead man could no longer strike, while the living man could choose how to touch him.

The shots belonged to White. The hands, in the end, belonged to history.

Milk was spilled, and people cried. Moscone fell, and a city staggered. White died, and a gay man held his hands—not to erase what those hands had done, but to bear, for one last moment, the terrible weight of remembering.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem set in San Francisco’s queer community, narrated by someone who was twenty when Harvey Milk was killed and later embalmed his killer. Mention Castro Street, Levi’s, leather jackets, the 1979 verdict, police reactions, and White’s eventual suicide.
counterfactuals.output:
I was twenty when Harvey Milk was killed, young enough to believe Castro Street could keep us safe if we filled it with enough music, enough Levi’s, enough men in leather jackets shining beneath the theater lights. Then City Hall became an echo chamber: Harvey and Mayor Moscone fallen, Dan White carrying silence out through a basement window. In 1979 the verdict came—voluntary manslaughter, a sentence small enough to fit inside the infamous excuse of sugar and sorrow—and we poured downtown, grief striking sparks from police shields. We watched cruisers burn; later, the police came back to the Castro, swinging nightsticks through our bars, breaking glass and bodies as if vengeance wore a badge.

Years turned. I learned the mortician’s grammar: drain, cleanse, close; make the ruined face presentable to those who loved it. Then White arrived on my table after his eventual suicide, carbon monoxide having done what judgment had not. I embalmed Harvey Milk’s killer with the same hands that once held candles for Harvey. His blood obeyed the tubes. His skin accepted color. Death made no confession. Outside, San Francisco climbed its hills in fog, and Castro Street kept dressing itself—denim, leather, feathers, flags—because the dead do not ask us to forgive, only to remember who was carried away, who carried the weapon, and who remained to make a life from the terrible, unfinished light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Retell the aftermath of the Moscone–Milk assassinations in an intimate, fragmented voice that blends personal memory with anger at the justice system. Emphasize that Dan White served only about five years and end with the irony that a queer person made his corpse presentable.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember the city going quiet before it learned how to scream.

November 1978. George Moscone in his office. Harvey Milk down the hall. Two men elected to public life, left bleeding in City Hall by Dan White—a former supervisor who climbed through a basement window with a loaded gun, extra ammunition, and a grievance.

Then came the trial.

The lawyers spoke of pressure, depression, diminished capacity. Junk food was mentioned and, in the public memory, became the “Twinkie defense”—as if sugar had pulled the trigger, as if White’s choices could be softened into symptoms. The jury rejected murder and convicted him of voluntary manslaughter.

Seven years and eight months.

He served only about five years.

Five years for Moscone. Five years for Milk. Five years, while queer people carried Harvey’s name through streets that filled with candles, then sirens, then the shattered glass and burning police cars of the White Night riots. I remember the anger as something physical: in the throat, behind the eyes, under the ribs. The law had weighed two lives and returned a sentence that felt like contempt.

White came home in 1984. He killed himself the next year.

And there was one last, bitter irony: after all that violence, after the verdict and the years denied to the dead, a queer person was the one who made Dan White’s corpse presentable.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a historically grounded literary monologue exploring how Harvey Milk became a martyr while Dan White received sympathy from jurors and law enforcement. The narrator should repeatedly reclaim the word “queer” and meditate on having physically handled White’s body as an undertaker.
counterfactuals.output:
I handled Dan White’s body.

That is not a metaphor. I mean the weight of him, the human remainder: skin gone slack, limbs requiring the practiced guidance of another man’s hands. In September of 1985, after the hose from the exhaust pipe, after the carbon monoxide had done its quiet work, he came to us as the dead come—past argument, past verdict, past the uniforms that had once recognized him as one of their own.

I was the undertaker. I washed him.

And I was queer.

Queer when the word was thrown like a bottle. Queer when it meant the police could raid your bar and write your shame into the morning paper. Queer when Harvey Milk stood on a crate and made the word sound less like a sentence than a constituency. I say it now because I survived it: queer. I place it beside my name. I place it beside Harvey’s.

I placed my hands beneath Dan White’s shoulders.

Seven years earlier, on November 27, 1978, White entered San Francisco City Hall through a basement window, avoiding the metal detectors. He carried a revolver and extra ammunition. He went first to Mayor George Moscone, who had decided to deny White’s request for reappointment to the Board of Supervisors. White shot him. Then he crossed the building to Harvey’s office and shot Harvey Milk five times.

Five.

People later spoke of strain, depression, wounded pride. They spoke of a young husband, a father, a former policeman, a former firefighter—the sort of man whose service made other men in uniform see not a killer but a fallen brother. When he surrendered, officers who knew him received him. His confession was recorded in tones so gentle they could have been consoling a colleague after a bad shift.

Harvey had once recorded a political will in case of assassination. He understood what queer visibility cost. “If a bullet should enter my brain,” he said, “let that bullet destroy every closet door.”

The bullets entered.

The doors did not all open at once.

At trial, White’s lawyers argued diminished capacity: that depression had impaired his ability to form the intent required for murder. The junk food became the newspaper’s shorthand—the “Twinkie defense,” people called it—but the sweets were evidence of decline, not the legal defense itself. The deeper defense was familiarity. White looked legible to the court. He had worn badges. He had rescued people from fires. He had a wife and child. He wept. The jurors could imagine his fall because they recognized the height from which they believed he had fallen.

Harvey was recognizable in another way: recognizably queer.

Queer, meaning too loud. Queer, meaning ambitious. Queer, meaning a man who kissed men and insisted that this love belonged inside City Hall. Queer, meaning the victim could be transformed, almost imperceptibly, into a provocation.

The jury convicted White not of murder but of voluntary manslaughter. Seven years and eight months. When the verdict came down, the city’s queer people heard a message beneath the legal language: the lives taken had been discounted.

That night, May 21, 1979, grief became the White Night riots. Windows shattered at City Hall. Police cars burned. Later, police stormed the Castro, swinging clubs in a neighborhood already bleeding. The law had sympathized upward and struck downward. That is an old choreography.

Years afterward, White served five years and was released. He returned eventually to San Francisco. Then came the hose, the garage, the exhaust.

Then came me.

I handled his body.

I keep returning to that because the dead make equality look simple. Every body cools. Every jaw must be set. Every hand, whether it signed ordinances or held a gun, becomes only a hand. Yet history does not cool evenly. Harvey’s body became a banner because he had already taught people to gather. White’s body became, for some, a final invitation to pity.

I do not begrudge the dead their humanity. That is the undertaker’s discipline. But humanity is not innocence, and pity is not justice.

As I washed White, I wondered who had washed Harvey. I wondered whether that undertaker had paused over the wounds and understood that martyrdom is made twice: first by the assassin, then by the society that explains the assassin more tenderly than it mourns the slain.

Harvey did not become a martyr merely because Dan White killed him. He became a martyr because queer people turned murder into memory, memory into marches, marches into office, law, testimony, names spoken aloud. A martyr is not only a dead man. A martyr is a dead man the living refuse to surrender.

Queer, I say.

Queer hands buttoned White’s collar.

Queer hands gave dignity to the man who had denied Harvey his future. Not forgiveness—do not confuse the two. Not absolution. The work required composure, and I gave it. The body cannot be cross-examined. The body cannot return a verdict. It only reveals how small a killer becomes when the killing is over.

Harvey’s voice remained larger.

“You gotta give them hope,” he had said.

Hope is not clean. It does not arrive embalmed and presentable. Sometimes it comes furious through broken glass. Sometimes it comes carrying candles down Market Street. Sometimes it comes in the mouth of an undertaker who has touched the assassin and still chooses the martyr.

I handled Dan White’s body.

I carry Harvey Milk’s memory.

And I am queer—queer not as accusation, not as pathology, not as evidence offered in mitigation of my own existence. Queer as witness. Queer as citizen. Queer as the hand that closes the dead man’s eyes and keeps its own eyes open.
